g1: Welcome back, scientist. This time we go deeper, into the human genome and into proteins, the machines it builds. Here is a map of how the ideas connect. Click any node to see what it means. Most people have never heard of half of these, and that's exactly what we'll fix.
g2: Your genome is about three billion letters per set, spread over twenty three chromosomes. Printed as novels, that is thousands of books. Each bar here is a chromosome, scaled to its real length. Sort them different ways and notice that long chromosomes are not always the ones with the most genes.
g3: Here is the surprise. Only about one and a half percent of your genome codes for proteins. Roughly half is repeats, old jumping genes like Alu and LINE one. So what is the rest doing? Scientists still argue, because the answer depends on what you mean by function. Try the three lenses.
g4: Any two people differ at roughly one letter in a thousand, millions of sites, but almost all are harmless. A few are different: whole chunks inserted, deleted or copied. Compare yourself to a stranger, a Neanderthal and a chimp, and watch the number of differences climb on a log scale.
g5: If every cell has the same genome, why is a neuron not a liver cell? Regulation. Enhancers, short switches far along the DNA, loop around to touch a gene's promoter and turn it on. Chemical tags like methylation can silence it. Choose a cell type, loop the DNA, and add methylation to see genes switch.
g6: Now to proteins. A protein is a chain of amino acids, chosen from just twenty. What matters is each one's side chain, its size and whether it loves or fears water. This map places all twenty by water preference and volume. That single property, hydrophobicity, drives almost everything about how a chain folds.
g7: Protein structure comes in four levels. First, the sequence, a string of amino acids. Second, local shapes: alpha helices and beta strands. Third, the full three dimensional fold of one chain. Fourth, several chains assembled together, like the four subunits of hemoglobin. Drag the slider to fold a real chain, then zoom all the way to atoms.
g8: Why is folding hard? In 1969 Cyrus Levinthal noticed that a chain has so many possible shapes that trying them at random would take longer than the age of the universe. Yet real proteins fold in milliseconds. The resolution is the energy funnel. Compare a random landscape to a funnel and drop a ball in.
g9: Let's watch hydrophobic collapse. This toy chain has water-fearing beads in orange and water-loving beads in blue. Release it, and the orange beads huddle together to hide from water, forming a core. Change the temperature, poke beads with your mouse, or add more chains and see what happens at high concentration.
g10: Folding can go wrong. One tiny change in hemoglobin, a glutamic acid swapped for a valine at position six of the beta chain, creates a sticky patch and causes sickle cell disease. Other proteins misfold into stacked beta sheets called amyloid fibrils, seen in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Build a fibril and inspect the sickle site.
g11: For fifty years, predicting a protein's shape from its sequence was a grand challenge. Experiments, X ray crystallography, NMR, and cryo electron microscopy, are slow and costly, so we know hundreds of thousands of structures but have hundreds of millions of sequences. Every two years, the Casp competition tested predictions blind. Walk along the timeline.
g12: How does AlphaFold work, at a high level? It first looks at a family of related sequences. When two positions mutate together across evolution, they probably touch in three dimensions. It turns those clues into a structure, and reports its own confidence, called p L D D T. Click the contact map, then compare prediction and experiment.
g13: Prediction opened the door to design. In 2024 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to David Baker for computational protein design, and to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for AlphaFold. Drug makers use structures to fit molecules into pockets. Here is an HIV protease with a real drug inside. Pull the ligand out and count the contacts.
g14: So is it solved? Not remotely. Here are the frontiers professionals care about: proteins that move, floppy disordered regions, folding pathways and speed, huge complexes, membrane proteins, predicting the effect of a mutation, understanding function, and designing new enzymes. Click each one to see why it is hard and where it stands.
g15: Final check. Eight questions across genomes, folding, and prediction. Score six or more to reach Frontier rank. Afterwards, take the cheat sheet, and the list of real databases where you can explore proteins, variants, and genomes yourself. You now know a good part of what you didn't know you didn't know.
